column1: What is the fundamental architectural difference between DAS and NAS in terms of locality assumptions?
column2: DAS assumes exclusive kernel ownership of a local block device with microsecond latency and no network coordination; NAS fractures this by requiring multiple independent kernels to coordinate access to shared storage over network latency orders of magnitude slower than local DRAM/NVMe.

column1: What are the three invariant challenges that define all network storage systems?
column2: 1) Network transparency (presenting remote storage with familiar POSIX semantics over unreliable networks), 2) Consistency model dilemma (strong vs. eventual consistency across distributed clients), 3) coordinating shared access across independent OS kernels.

column1: What is the core invariant of any storage engine, and what architectural mechanisms enforce it?
column2: Durability: once an application receives write acknowledgment, data must survive all single points of failure within design parameters. Enforced via RAID (disk failure tolerance), write-ahead logging (crash recovery), and copy-on-write systems like ZFS (eliminating update-in-place hazards).

column1: Why does RAID use striping, mirroring, and parity, and what is the core mathematical trade-off?
column2: Striping parallelizes I/O, mirroring duplicates data for redundancy, parity computes algebraic checksums for reconstruction. Given N drives and K tolerated failures, the system must store sufficient redundant information to reconstruct lost blocks, trading capacity and performance against reliability.

column1: How does NFSv3 statelessness differ from SMB/CIFS statefulness in terms of failover behavior?
column2: NFSv3 maintains minimal server-side state, so a replacement server can assume a failed node's IP/volumes with brief client-side retry interruption. SMB/CIFS maintains extensive session state (open handles, oplocks, auth contexts), so server failure invalidates state and forces clients to re-establish sessions, often surfacing errors to applications.

column1: In a dual-controller active-passive NAS setup, how does redundancy transform failure probability mathematically?
column2: If a single controller has a 2% annual failure rate (98% availability, ~7.3 days downtime/year), adding an independent redundant controller reduces simultaneous failure probability to ~0.04% (product of independent failure rates), assuming perfect detection and instantaneous failover.

column1: What are the three axiomatic security invariants of a multi-tenant NAS system?
column2: 1) Identity must be externally authoritative (no credentials owned solely by the NAS), 2) Authorization must be explicit (access only via explicit policy grant, never by default), 3) Confidentiality must be layered (data unreadable across network, disk, and hypervisor attack surfaces).

column1: Why is NFSv3's UID/GID-based authentication considered a documented security model rather than a bug?
column2: NFSv3 credentials are raw UID/GID pairs asserted by the client kernel with no cryptographic verification, so any client with root access can forge any identity. This honor-system model is by design, which is why NFSv3 was traditionally confined to trusted private networks.

column1: How does NFSv4 with RPCSEC_GSS/Kerberos eliminate the NFSv3 impersonation vulnerability?
column2: It replaces the honor-system UID/GID model with a cryptographically signed Kerberos ticket issued by the KDC to a verified principal, eliminating the ability to forge identity via effective UID manipulation.

column1: What is the security weakness progression across NTLMv1, NTLMv2, and Kerberos over SMB3?
column2: NTLMv1 uses a 56-bit DES challenge-response breakable by brute force in minutes; NTLMv2 improves hash construction but remains vulnerable to relay attacks; Kerberos over SMB3 solves relay attacks via mutual authentication where both client and server cryptographically prove identity before data transfer.

column1: What causes 'bit rot' in storage systems and why does its probability scale with capacity and time?
column2: Bit rot is silent corruption from cosmic rays flipping charge states in DRAM or magnetic domain decay on platters. Because corruption events are probabilistic per-bit, larger capacity and longer retention periods increase the cumulative likelihood of undetected sector failures (e.g., a 10-drive, 100TB array over 5 years will almost certainly see multiple failures).

column1: Why does SSD write amplification eventually render a device read-only?
column2: Repeated program-erase cycles degrade NAND cells; write amplification increases the actual number of writes beyond logical writes, accelerating wear until the reserve (spare) block pool is exhausted, at which point the device can no longer remap worn cells and becomes read-only.
